trial_name: VITdAL-ICU — High-Dose Vitamin D3 in Critically Ill Patients with Vitamin D Deficiency (2014)
citation: Amrein K, Schnedl C, Holl A, Riedl R, Christopher KB, Pachler C, et al. Effect of high-dose vitamin D3 on hospital length of stay in critically ill patients with vitamin D deficiency: the VITdAL-ICU randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014;312(15):1520-1530
one_liner: High-dose vitamin D3 did not reduce hospital length of stay; a mortality benefit was seen only in the severe deficiency subgroup (≤12 ng/mL), requiring confirmation.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with 25(OH)D ≤20 ng/mL, anticipated ICU stay ≥48 hours
pico.intervention: Enteral cholecalciferol 540,000 IU loading dose + 90,000 IU monthly ×5 months
pico.outcome: Primary: hospital length of stay; secondary: ICU length of stay, mortality (ICU, 28-day, hospital, 6-month), biochemical correction

background.existing_knowledge: Vitamin D deficiency is common in critically ill patients, linked observationally to higher mortality, infections, and longer stay. Confounding and reverse causality limit causal inference. Vitamin D replacement is inexpensive and biologically plausible.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty about optimal dose, timing, and whether correction improves clinical outcomes, particularly in severe deficiency. Prior interventional evidence was limited and heterogeneous.
background.hypothesis: Rapid correction of vitamin D deficiency using high-dose cholecalciferol reduces hospital length of stay compared with placebo.

methods.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center, stratified, parallel-group
methods.setting: 5 adult ICUs (medical, surgical, neurological, cardiothoracic) at Medical University of Graz, Austria; enrolment May 2010–Mar 2012

inclusion: Enteral access and able to receive study drug
exclusion: Hypercalcaemia (total calcium >10.6 mg/dL or ionised Ca >5.4 mg/dL)

methods.intervention: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) 540,000 IU enteral loading dose, then 90,000 IU monthly ×5 months; background standard vitamin D (≈200 IU/day) allowed but additional supplementation discouraged
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors); pharmacy-controlled allocation
methods.sample_size_power: Planned n=490 to detect 2-day reduction in mean hospital length of stay (two-sided α=0.05, power 80%); analysed 475 (modified ITT)
methods.follow_up: In-hospital outcomes; mortality assessed at ICU discharge, 28 days, hospital discharge, 6 months; biochemical follow-up at days 3, 7, 28, and 6 months; functional outcomes at 6 months

headline_bullets: Primary endpoint neutral: median hospital LOS 19.3 vs 20.1 days (P=0.98).
ICU LOS unchanged (10.7 vs 9.6 days, P=0.38).
All-cause mortality numerically lower with vitamin D3 but not statistically significant overall (6-month HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.58–1.04, P=0.09).
In severe deficiency (≤12 ng/mL), hospital mortality was significantly reduced (28.6% vs 46.1%; HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.35–0.90, P=0.01, interaction P=0.04).
Biochemical separation was large (day 7 mean 25(OH)D 35.5 vs 14.5 ng/mL, P<0.001); 52% of vitamin D3 group reached >30 ng/mL by day 7.

subgroup_table.subgroup: Severe vitamin D deficiency (25(OH)D ≤12 ng/mL) — Hospital mortality
Severe vitamin D deficiency (25(OH)D ≤12 ng/mL) — 28-day mortality

safety: Hypercalcemia (>10.6 mg/dL) at 6 months: 4/37 (11%) vitamin D3 vs 1/43 (2%) placebo (subset with labs).

domains.notes: Computer-generated sequence (block size 8), stratified by ICU type and sex; pharmacy-controlled packaging ensures concealment.
Double-blind with matched preparations; mortality outcomes are objective; hospital LOS is objective but influenced by discharge processes.
Modified ITT: 492 randomised, 480 received treatment, 475 analysed (237 vs 238). 9 vitamin D3 patients excluded vs 3 placebo; risk of bias if exclusions prognostic.
Biochemical separation confirmed (day 7 25(OH)D 35.5 vs 14.5 ng/mL); only 52% of vitamin D3 group reached >30 ng/mL, reflecting variability.
Groups well matched (age, SAPS II, mechanical ventilation, norepinephrine use).
Broad ICU case-mix increases heterogeneity; randomisation occurred median 2.1 days after ICU admission, potentially late for early immunomodulation.
Long-term biochemical and functional data available in subsets (e.g., month 6 labs: 37 vs 43), limiting precision for safety and longer outcomes.
Primary analysis underpowered (n=475 vs planned 490); mortality analyses secondary; subgroup testing interaction P=0.04 but still hypothesis-generating.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong internal validity: robust randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding and biochemical separation, but limited by modified ITT, incomplete long-term data and an organisational-sensitive primary endpoint.

domains.notes: Single-center, 100% White European adult ICU cohort with documented deficiency (≤20 ng/mL) and anticipated stay ≥48 hours; may not generalise to more diverse ethnic groups, shorter-stay ICUs, or ICUs with different discharge practices.
Enteral high-dose cholecalciferol is inexpensive and feasible, but routine ICU screening for 25(OH)D and rapid treatment pathways vary. Benefit may depend on deficiency severity and timing.

external_validity.verdict: Reasonably applicable to similar tertiary ICUs caring for vitamin D–deficient patients, but generalisability constrained by single-centre design, homogeneous ethnicity, and length-of-stay dependence on local discharge practices.

strengths: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled with pharmacy allocation.
Large ICU vitamin D trial with stratification by ICU type/sex reducing imbalance.
Robust serial biochemical measurements clearly separating groups.
Objective mortality outcomes with 6-month follow-up; functional outcomes collected.
limitations: Primary endpoint (hospital LOS) sensitive to discharge processes and competing risk of death.
Modified ITT (475/492) risks bias; more vitamin D3 patients excluded.
Underpowered for mortality; mortality benefit confined to severe deficiency subgroup.
Long-term safety data limited to small subsets.

critical_appraisal.summary: Well-designed but single-centre trial showing biochemical correction without reduction in length of stay; mortality signal in severe deficiency is hypothesis-generating only.
weaknesses: Length-of-stay primary endpoint sensitive to local practice

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine high-dose cholecalciferol to shorten hospital stay in vitamin D–deficient ICU patients is not supported. The severe deficiency subgroup signal (≤12 ng/mL) is hypothesis-generating and warrants further trials targeting profound deficiency and patient-centred outcomes.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not change practice for most ICU patients. High-dose vitamin D3 quickly normalizes levels but does not reduce length of stay. Any mortality benefit appears limited to severe deficiency and remains unproven.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with 25(OH)D ≤20 ng/mL, particularly those with very low levels (≤12 ng/mL).
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Vitamin D is harmful or should be withheld; correction of severe deficiency may still matter, but routine screening/treatment for LOS reduction is not justified.
implementation_caveats: Routine screening and high-dose bolus are not supported for ICU-wide practice.
If targeted to severely deficient patients, close monitoring of calcium and falls may be needed.
Results from larger multicentre trials (e.g., VIOLET) did not confirm benefit.

controversies.notes: Hospital length of stay is multifactorial and influenced by discharge processes; a neutral LOS finding does not exclude biologically meaningful effects on mortality or organ dysfunction, but makes the trial vulnerable to context-specific practice variation.
Excluding 17/492 randomised patients (5 consent withdrawals; 12 not treated) can bias effect estimates if exclusions correlate with prognosis, particularly when mortality is an outcome.

Mortality benefit was confined to 25(OH)D ≤12 ng/mL (hospital mortality interaction P=0.04); despite interaction testing, multiplicity and subgroup fragility limit certainty, and this subgroup effect is not a sufficient basis for practice change without confirmation.

In vitamin D–deficient critically ill adults randomised to a single enteral 540,000 IU vitamin D3 dose vs placebo within 12 hours of ICU admission decision, 90-day mortality was 23.5% vs 20.6% (RR 1.17; 95% CI 0.96 to 1.43; P=0.26), and the trial was stopped early for futility, challenging the generalisability of subgroup mortality benefits seen in VITdAL-ICU.

An updated meta-analysis of randomised trials reported reduced overall mortality with vitamin D administration (RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.97; P=0.03), shorter ICU length of stay (mean difference −3.13 days; 95% CI −5.36 to −0.90; P=0.006) and shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −5.07 days; 95% CI −9.68 to −0.47; P=0.03); heterogeneity across dosing strategies, routes, baseline deficiency definitions and trial quality remains a central interpretive challenge.

context_related_trials.relation: A subsequent larger multicentre RCT that used a single 540,000 IU vitamin D3 dose within 12 hours of ICU admission; found no benefit on 90-day mortality (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.96–1.43), stopped early for futility, challenging the subgroup mortality signal in VITdAL-ICU.

unresolved_questions: Does high-dose vitamin D3 improve mortality in patients with severe deficiency (<12 ng/mL) if given early?
What is the optimal dosing strategy (bolus vs daily) and timing?
Does vitamin D administration affect patient-centred outcomes beyond length of stay?
Confirming long-term safety of high-dose bolus (hypercalcemia, falls, fractures) in larger populations.

numbers_to_remember: Primary hospital LOS neutral: 19.3 vs 20.1 days (P=0.98)
Severe deficiency hospital mortality HR 0.56 (0.35–0.90), interaction P=0.04
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: High-dose vitamin D3 corrects deficiency but does not shorten stay; any mortality benefit is unconfirmed and limited to severe deficiency.
